headline: Rice Scientists Develop Filter 100x Faster at Destroying Forever Chemicals
meta_description: Rice University's new copper-aluminum filter destroys PFAS 'forever chemicals' 100 times faster, offering hope for contaminated drinking water worldwide.
summary_short: Researchers at Rice University have created a copper-aluminum filter that destroys PFAS—persistent chemicals linked to health risks—far more rapidly than existing method…
body:
A new copper-aluminum filter developed at Rice University can destroy PFAS—the persistent chemicals known as "forever chemicals"—100 times faster than conventional approaches, according to recent research.

Michael Wong, director of the PFAS Research Center at Rice University's Water Institute, leads the effort to engineer the material for capturing a wider range of these contaminants. PFAS accumulate in drinking water and the environment, posing significant health concerns. The challenge lies not just in creating effective solutions, but in scaling them for real-world use.

PFAS researcher Laura Orlando emphasized the broader need: "We're going to need as many technologies as we can possibly find to deal with PFAS in drinking water, and if this works to scale on wastewater, then it would be really something to pay attention to." The filter's potential to work at scale on wastewater treatment represents a significant step toward tackling this pervasive contamination problem globally.
quick_facts: Rice University copper-aluminum filter destroys PFAS 100 times faster
Michael Wong leads PFAS Research Center at Rice Water Institute
Technology could expand to capture wider range of PFAS chemicals
Potential application in wastewater treatment at industrial scale
